title: Sensor and Shipping Data
answer: Sensor and shipping data as alternative data covers physical-world signals from vessel transponders, port sensors, weather stations and cargo telemetry, used to estimate trade flows, commodity supply, congestion and industrial activity. crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Sensor and shipping data as alternative data covers physical-world signals from vessel transponders, port sensors, weather stations and cargo telemetry, used to estimate trade flows, commodity supply, congestion and industrial activity. It sits within alternative data because it is not standard financial reporting but can inform economic analysis ahead of official statistics. The topic includes data from maritime, rail, trucking and warehousing sensors where they bear on the movement of goods.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The data runs on Automatic Identification System transponders carried by ships, satellite and terrestrial receivers, port and canal cameras, and internet-connected sensors on containers and vessels. Ingest pipelines normalize timestamps, positions and identifiers, then store the records in cloud object storage and stream processing systems. Geospatial databases support route queries, zone entry and exit detection, and distance calculations. Many providers also maintain vessel registries and historical archives that link a ship's identity to its owner, flag and cargo history.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: Analysts clean AIS pings by removing duplicates and implausible positions, then match vessel identifiers to ownership, charter and cargo manifest records. They build features such as port call counts, dwell times, deadweight tonnage, route deviations and average speed, and aggregate them by port, region or commodity. Statistical models and machine learning are used to nowcast trade volumes, freight rates or inventory levels from these features. Sensor fusion with weather data and satellite imagery can fill gaps when AIS coverage is sparse.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Data is usually purchased or licensed from commercial providers, with contract terms that restrict redistribution and may limit use in trading or research. Risks include AIS spoofing, receiver gaps, re-identification of individual vessels or cargo owners, and conflicts with sanctions or privacy rules when tracking specific ships. Provenance should record the sensor source, timestamp, and any interpolation or imputation applied to the raw signal. Analysts also need to document the version of the vessel registry and the matching logic used.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: More satellite constellations and lower-cost internet-connected sensors are increasing coverage and revisit rates, while machine learning is being used to infer cargo types and detect dark fleet activity such as transponder shutdowns. Integration with port digital twins and customs data may improve short-term trade estimates and reduce reliance on monthly official statistics. The field is moving toward real-time, vessel-level economic indicators that can be updated daily or hourly.
